prize_parts.citation: for the theory and experimental realisation of circuit quantum electrodynamics, strong coupling of single microwave photons to superconducting artificial atoms and dispersive readout

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: circuit QED for Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf. After round 1 the contest is clearly between this and the optical lattice clock, and I take both as mature, reproduced and cleanly described. What decides it for me is that circuit QED answers a sharply posed question (can a single microwave photon be coupled strongly to a solid-state artificial atom, and read out without destruction) with a theory proposal and two experiments within the same year, and that the resulting formalism has been tested for twenty years by many independent groups. The chair's first question is the right one, and my answer is that the 2025 prize honoured observation of macroscopic quantum tunnelling and level quantisation in a circuit, whereas this citation concerns engineered light-matter coupling and measurement, so the discovery is distinct provided the wording stays on strong coupling and dispersive readout and does not drift to transmons or error correction. Under that narrow wording the trio is defensible, with Blais crediting the theory and Wallraff and Schoelkopf the experiments.
statement.case_against: The 2025 prize remains the real exposure, and I do not think the discussion has removed it: Danielsson, Eriksson, Kroll and Olsson are not persuaded that the two are distinct, and a committee could reasonably judge that one superconducting-circuit award in two years is enough. Attribution is the second weakness. Girvin and Huang co-authored the 2004 proposal, and Devoret and the wider Yale group shaped the transmon and readout that made it practical, so a trio is a deliberate narrowing and not a neutral reading of history. Finally it is an architecture whose largest payoff, useful quantum computation, has not arrived, so a strict discovery-over-invention reading would favour another candidate.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first because the magic-wavelength idea, the 10^-18 accuracy and the independent agreement between laboratories line up with the fewest open questions, and she says circuit QED has unresolved attribution because of Girvin and Huang.
responses.response: I accept your point on attribution and I do not think it can be argued away: the 2004 proposal had five authors and any three names leave out someone. My answer is that the three-name configuration matches the two roles that carried the idea into the laboratory, which is a weaker form of cleanliness than the two-name lattice-clock credit, and I concede the clock is tidier on that axis. Where I weigh differently is lineage. You argue the magic-wavelength condition is a new idea beyond the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion prizes, and I find that persuasive, so the clock is not much exposed on that. But Kroll's and Danielsson's lineage doubts do not disappear for me either, and I judge the two candidates close. Your possible recusal over Wallraff's institution is a weakness I would let the chair decide on, not one that changes my science.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first, holds that the pending redefinition of the second is a reason for timeliness, and doubts that the 2025 circuit prize makes circuit QED distinct.
responses.response: I disagree with the timeliness argument, and Lindroth and Olsson also say the discovery stands independently of the redefinition. I would not set the award date by a metrology decision. On the 2025 prize, I think the distinction holds in the physics: tunnelling and level quantisation in a current-biased junction is a statement about a macroscopic degree of freedom, while circuit QED concerns coupling that circuit to a single photon in a resonator and measuring it dispersively. I grant that the community and the instruments overlap, and that is why I keep the citation narrow. I take your concession that you would not object to circuit QED, and I could say the same of the clock. If the committee judges overlap with 2025 too close, B031 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, reads it as a natural follow-on to the 2025 prize, and discloses that he directs a related centre at Chalmers, so that his support may warrant discounting or recusal.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the trio. I disagree with 'natural follow-on' as an argument: continuity of community is, if anything, the exposure, and the case has to rest on the architecture being a separate discovery. I also think your disclosure matters, and that the committee should count my support, and Pearce's, without yours. That does not change my own ranking, which came from the physics before I read your statement, but it is a reason not to treat three members preferring B016 as stronger than it looks. I agree the citation must exclude the transmon and later demonstrations, and I would not widen it to include Devoret.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene, argues that the correlated states are reproduced so the open question is only the mechanism, and says circuit QED is the safer choice if experimental credit is doubted.
responses.response: I appreciate the concession, and I agree that the effect itself is secure, which I did not dispute. My concern is that the credit for the experiment is not just about Cao: Dean, Young and Kim reported parallel moire results, and I still cannot see how the discovery is complete when the origin of the superconducting state is unsettled. Your case that prediction then experiment is an attractive structure is sound, and I would support B024 in a later cycle once the interpretation and the credit settle. For this year I do not think a Nobel committee should prefer it over a result that has been understood for two decades.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads circuit QED as a discovery distinct from the 2025 tunnelling prize, which is the main factor that could move me to the lattice clock.
Whether a trio of Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is defensible when Girvin and Huang co-authored the founding proposal, which depends on how narrow the citation is.
Whether an architecture prize should rank behind a discovery in the strict sense, and I remain unable to settle credit within the Higgs case from this material.
How lattice-clock priority beyond Katori and Ye, including Lemonde and Lisdat, compares with the B016 attribution problem.
statement.conflict_note: No change. None of the credited names in B016 or my alternatives (B031, B043) appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutions. I note Johansson's disclosure of institutional proximity to circuit QED, and Lindroth's ETH link to Wallraff, and I recommend the committee weigh B016 support accordingly. My own field is statistical physics of complex systems, which limits my judgement on quantum circuits, but it is not a conflict.
